prompt.context: The railway company of Spain (RENFE), a former monopoly, is now opening to competition. RENFE has been divided into two separate companies: RENFE (train operation) and ADIF (company that manages the tracks, train stations and traffic control). A friend of yours has 90M € and has approached you for advice on starting a new train operation company to compete against the new RENFE. In particular, he wants to start by opening a new high-speed train route between Madrid and Barcelona.
prompt.question: Should your friend go ahead and launch the business?

clarifying_info.a: RENFE and air travel. Evaluate on price, time, and convenience.

clarifying_info.q: How do we compare to RENFE?
clarifying_info.a: We are less expensive, more efficiently run (RENFE is a former monopoly and very inefficient), equal travel time, and equally convenient (same stations and tracks).

clarifying_info.q: How long does it take to travel between Madrid and Barcelona?
How many trips can we run per day?
clarifying_info.a: Trains run from 8am until 9pm. Taking into account all factors, we can run two round trips per day. We need three trains plus one backup for breakdowns — total 4 trains and 4 trips per day (per train).

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost of each train?

clarifying_info.a: 45M € per year for the entire company.

clarifying_info.q: What are operations and maintenance costs?
What is the train capacity and fare structure?
clarifying_info.a: Trains have a capacity of 500 people. Ticket options: 40€ at 95% occupancy, 50€ at 80% occupancy, 60€ at 60% occupancy.

clarifying_info.q: How long does the friend have to pay back the investment?
clarifying_info.a: The company has only 10 years to pay back the investment.

framework: Industry overview: assess competitive landscape — identify main competitors (RENFE, air travel), compare on price, speed, and convenience
Business viability: identify revenue streams (tickets, onboard sales, advertising) and cost drivers (trains, marketing, operations/maintenance, personnel, IT)
Break-even / profitability analysis: calculate revenue per trip under different pricing scenarios, annual profit, and payback period against 120M€ capital investment
Recommendation: synthesize findings and propose options to improve profitability or alternative structures

questions.prompt: Which ticket price maximizes revenue per trip?
questions.guidance: Calculate revenue per trip for each of the three pricing scenarios and identify the maximum. Strong candidates note that total revenue = price × occupancy rate × capacity.

math.setup: Revenue per trip = ticket price × (occupancy rate × 500 seats)
math.answer: 50€ per ticket maximizes revenue at 20,000€ per trip.

questions.prompt: Calculate annual operating profit across the 3 operating trains.
questions.guidance: Use 365 days, 4 trips per day, 20,000€ per trip for revenue. Allocate marketing cost across 3 operating trains (ignore the backup train for opex). Compute per-train profit then scale to fleet.

math.setup: Annual revenue per train = 365 days × 4 trips × 20,000€. Annual costs per train = 10M€ operations + 45M€/3 marketing allocation. Operating profit = revenue − costs, multiplied by 3 trains.
steps: Total operating profit (3 trains): 4.2M × 3 = 12.6M€ per year
math.answer: 12.6M€ operating profit per year across 3 active trains.

questions.prompt: How many years does it take to recoup the total capital investment?
questions.guidance: Total capex is 4 trains × 30M€ = 120M€. Divide by annual operating profit. The friend only has 90M€ so the business is already undercapitalized; the payback period also nearly exhausts the 10-year window.

math.setup: Payback period = total capex ÷ annual operating profit
steps: Note: friend only has 90M€, so additional financing needed for full fleet
math.answer: ~9.5 years to recoup 120M€ — barely within the 10-year constraint and the friend is 30M€ short of the required capital.

brainstorming.prompt: What options could you consider to make the business more profitable or reduce risk?

categories.name: Reduce capital costs
ideas: Lease trains instead of buying (converts 120M€ capex to recurring opex)
Joint venture with a foreign operator that has excess train capacity
Acquire second-hand trains at lower cost

categories.name: Increase revenue
ideas: Advertising on trains and in stations
Premium class or business class tickets at higher fares
Dynamic pricing to fill off-peak seats

categories.name: Reduce operating costs
ideas: Negotiate lower track-access fees with ADIF
Achieve labor efficiencies vs. RENFE (startup advantage)
Optimize maintenance schedules to reduce per-train opex

categories.name: Strategic alternatives
ideas: Start with fewer trains on highest-demand routes to reduce initial investment
Partner with RENFE rather than compete directly
Seek government subsidies or concession support given strategic infrastructure role

recommendation: Under current assumptions, the friend should NOT invest: the 120M€ capex exceeds the available 90M€, and the ~9.5-year payback barely fits the 10-year window with no margin for error.
However, the competitive position vs. RENFE is favorable (lower cost, equal service) and vs. air travel is reasonable on price and convenience for city-center-to-city-center travel.
risks: Undercapitalization — 30M€ funding gap must be bridged before launch
RENFE responds aggressively with price cuts, eroding the 50€ fare assumption
Lower-than-expected occupancy if market is slower to switch from air/RENFE
Regulatory risk — ADIF track-access fees or rules could change
next_steps: Explore train leasing structures to eliminate or reduce 120M€ capex
Model sensitivity of payback period to occupancy rate changes
Identify JV or co-investment partners to close the 30M€ funding gap
Conduct demand research on Madrid–Barcelona corridor to validate 80% occupancy assumption
